name: Sleep diary

card.summary: A day-by-day log of bed and wake times, naps, caffeine and sleep quality kept for one to two weeks, used to improve sleep and with it skin, energy and training recovery.
card.note: Self-reported; clinicians pair it with other measures when diagnosing sleep disorders.

quick.overview:
A sleep diary is a simple record of when you go to bed, fall asleep, wake and nap, plus things like caffeine, alcohol, exercise and mood. People in lifestyle-focused looksmaxxing keep one because better, more regular sleep supports skin, mood, energy and recovery from training, and a diary shows patterns that are otherwise hard to notice.

Clinically it is a standard tool in assessing insomnia, and a standardised version, the Consensus Sleep Diary, was published in 2012. Reviews describe it as simple, cheap and easy to use, with the limitation that it relies on self-report.
quick.how: The log is kept for one to two weeks on paper, in a spreadsheet or an app, filled in each morning (and sometimes evening). Entries typically cover intended and actual wake time, time to fall asleep, night awakenings, naps, substances, exercise and a quality rating. Users then look for patterns and discuss them with a clinician if sleep problems persist.
quick.risks: Keeping a diary is low-risk. Some people find that watching their sleep closely increases worry about it, and recorded estimates can be inaccurate or incomplete. It records sleep rather than treating it.

lead: A sleep diary is a self-reported record of sleep and wake times and related factors, usually kept for several weeks by the sleeper or a caregiver. Wikipedia lists typical entries such as intended and actual wake time, naps, exercise, medications, caffeine and alcohol, evening meals, pre-bed activities, time trying to fall asleep, night awakenings and sleep quality.[1]

People who work on their appearance use it as the first step in sleep optimisation: regular, sufficient sleep is tied in these communities to clearer skin, less puffiness, steadier mood and better recovery from lifting, so logging habits is a way to see what helps or hurts.

In clinical practice the diary is a core tool for assessing insomnia. Reviews describe it as a prospective self-monitoring method used to quantify severity, track change in treatment and check adherence to a schedule, and a 2012 consensus sleep diary standardised its format.[1][2][3]

chain: Log bed times, wake times, naps and habits
Spot patterns that cut sleep or make it irregular
angle.text: The diary does not change sleep by itself; it shows which habits line up with good and poor nights so a person can adjust them. Better sleep is then connected, by users, to improved skin, energy and training recovery.

paras: Diaries are often handwritten on graph paper, one week per page, or kept in spreadsheets, databases or dedicated apps.[1] A clinician reviewing a diary can compute measures such as time to fall asleep, time awake in the night and overall sleep time. Smartphone health apps also offer sleep logging, a feature discussed on Hacker News.[4]

A 2023 review in the Danish medical journal describes the sleep diary alongside questionnaires and objective tests as part of the multimodal work-up of sleep disorders.[5][6] Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia, described as the recommended first-line treatment in a review of insomnia in older adults, uses diary data for components such as sleep restriction and stimulus control.[7] A JAMA review also covers the assessment and treatment of insomnia.[8]
Wikipedia lists advantages as simplicity, low cost and ease of use, and drawbacks as inaccurate or incomplete recording and scoring errors, especially on paper.[1]
Lifestyle-oriented users keep a diary for one to two weeks to establish a baseline before changing bedtime, caffeine timing, light exposure or other habits, then compare.

The Consensus Sleep Diary paper in Sleep (2012) describes the development of a standardised prospective self-monitoring instrument.[3] Sleep diaries were used as measures in many insomnia trials, including trials of behavioural versus drug treatment, online cognitive behavioural therapy and brief behavioural treatment in older adults.[9][10][11] Research on whether keeping a diary improves skin or appearance specifically has not been published.

timeline.event: The Consensus Sleep Diary is published to standardise prospective sleep self-monitoring.[3]
